q: Define rotator cuff tendinopathy, and explain why the definition is phrased around load rather than damage.
a:
A painful, load-related disorder of the rotator cuff tendons and surrounding tissues, in which demand has exceeded the tendon's capacity to tolerate it.

The phrasing matters clinically. A damage-based definition implies something broken that must be repaired, and leads to rest, imaging and surgical thinking. A capacity-based definition identifies two modifiable variables — reduce demand temporarily, raise capacity permanently — and both are things you can prescribe. It also explains why structural findings correlate so poorly with symptoms: the problem is a mismatch, not a lesion.

q: Why was "subacromial impingement syndrome" abandoned, and what replaced it?
a:
It embeds a causal mechanism — mechanical compression under the acromion — that placebo-controlled surgery disproved. If compression were the cause, removing bone should outperform a sham operation. It does not.

The preferred term is rotator cuff-related shoulder pain (RCRSP), which names the region without claiming to know the tissue; subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) is an acceptable alternative. The term also shapes the patient: "impingement" tells them something is being crushed and invites a request for decompression.

q: What should you look for in the weeks before onset, and why do patients fail to report it?
a:
A spike in load — a new job or task, a return to sport, a DIY project, a holiday with a heavy bag, covering a colleague's shift — typically three to six weeks upstream of the first symptom.

Patients report the moment pain appeared, not the accumulation that produced it, and by then they have stopped connecting the two. Ask "what were you doing in the month before it started?" rather than "what happened?" — the latter reliably produces "nothing", and you will wrongly conclude it arose spontaneously.

q: Why does returning to a previous activity level so often trigger symptoms?
a:
Because it combines both halves of the mismatch: the load returns to its old level while capacity has fallen during the break.

This is the spike patients most reliably fail to report, because in their own account they did nothing new — they simply went back to normal. A layoff from training, a period of illness, a long holiday or a lighter work rota all set it up.

q: What are the rotator cable and crescent?
a:
The cable is a thickened band running perpendicular to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons, from the biceps anchor anteriorly to the inferior infraspinatus posteriorly. The crescent is the thinner tissue it spans.

The arrangement works like a suspension bridge, with the cable carrying load across the thinner membrane beneath it.

q: What is the clinical consequence of the cable–crescent arrangement?
a:
If the cable is intact, load is transmitted around a crescent defect rather than through it.

This is why some tears remain functionally compensated, and why tear size alone predicts function poorly — a crescent tear with an intact cable behaves very differently from one that has disrupted the cable. It is part of the explanation for patients who have a substantial tear on imaging and near-normal function.

q: Why is the enthesis a common site of degeneration and tear initiation?
a:
It is a graded transition between materials of vastly different stiffness — tendon to bone. That gradient exists precisely to spread stress across the junction, which inevitably makes it a stress concentrator.

Anywhere that stress concentrates is where degenerative change accumulates and where tears begin.

q: Why does surgical repair not restore the enthesis, and what follows clinically?
a:
Repair does not recreate the stiffness gradient — it heals with fibrovascular scar, which is weaker than the original transition.

Two consequences follow: it is the biological explanation for re-tear rates, and for the roughly three-month delay before strengthening after repair. Worth knowing when a patient asks why post-operative rehabilitation is so slow compared with other surgery.

q: What does the rotator interval contain, and what do those structures form?
a:
The triangular gap between the anterior border of supraspinatus and the superior border of subscapularis, containing the coracohumeral ligament, the superior glenohumeral ligament, and the long head of biceps passing through to the supraglenoid tubercle.

Together these form the biceps pulley — the sling that holds the long head in its groove.

q: What does a medially subluxed long head of biceps on ultrasound indicate?
a:
A subscapularis lesion. The pulley has failed, and subscapularis is part of that pulley.

It is not an isolated biceps problem, and treating the displacement without looking for its cause misses the actual lesion. This is a good example of an imaging finding that should redirect your examination rather than conclude it.

q: How should the long head of biceps be regarded in cuff disease, and how is it tested?
a:
As a companion diagnosis, not a competing one. It is richly innervated, frequently inflamed alongside cuff disease, and a common reason anterior shoulder pain persists after the cuff itself has settled.

Test with Speed's test and palpation in the groove with the arm in 10° internal rotation, which rotates the groove anteriorly under your finger. If anterior pain outlasts the cuff programme, reconsider the biceps rather than assuming the programme failed.

q: What is the normal acromiohumeral interval, and what does narrowing indicate?
a:
Normally 7–14 mm. Below 7 mm indicates superior migration of the humeral head.

That is a marker of a large or massive tear with loss of the coronal force couple — not of simple tendinopathy. It is a cheap, immediately available piece of information on a true AP radiograph, and it changes the conversation before any soft-tissue imaging is ordered.

q: What is the function of the subacromial bursa, and why does a subacromial injection target it?
a:
The bursa's job is to let the cuff glide under the coracoacromial arch with minimal friction. It is the largest bursa in the body, synovial, densely innervated, and capable of thickening and producing effusion.

That makes it both a major pain source and the correct injection target — which is why the needle goes into the bursa and never into the tendon.

q: What mechanical problem must the shoulder solve, and what pays the bill?
a:
The glenohumeral joint has the largest range of motion in the body and almost no passive stability — a large humeral head on a shallow glenoid, with a capsule that must stay lax through mid-range or you could not reach.

There is no bony cup and nothing holding the joint by shape. So the price of that range is that something must pay for stability actively, every second the arm is in use — and that something is the rotator cuff. This is why dynamic muscular stabilisation is not optional here as it is at the hip.

q: Define concavity-compression.
a:
The cuff compresses the convex humeral head into the concave glenoid. Press a ball into a socket and the socket resists the ball sliding out: the deeper the socket and the harder you press, the more shear force it takes to translate the head.

The labrum contributes by increasing the effective depth of the socket; capsule and ligaments add passive restraint.

q: What is the key concept that concavity-compression establishes about the cuff?
a:
The cuff is a compressor before it is a mover.

It does not simply rotate the humerus — it generates the compressive force that keeps the joint stable throughout movement. Every other conclusion in this chapter about cuff dysfunction follows from this one: when the cuff fails, what is primarily lost is stability, not a particular movement.

q: Why can deltoid not elevate the arm without the cuff?
a:
In the early arc deltoid's line of pull is largely vertical. If the head were free to slide, deltoid would simply drag it upward against the acromion.

The cuff prevents this by compressing the head into the socket and pulling inferiorly, so deltoid's force is converted into rotation about a fixed point rather than translation. The cuff and deltoid are not competing — the cuff creates the condition under which deltoid can work at all.

q: How much superior translation occurs during normal elevation?
a:
Only about 1–2 mm. The centre of rotation stays remarkably still.

That fixed point is the fulcrum, and its stability is the measure of whether the cuff is doing its primary job. Significant superior migration is characteristic of large or massive tears, not of simple tendinopathy.

q: Why should you stop teaching that supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of abduction?
a:
Because it is wrong on three counts: supraspinatus is active across the whole arc, its dominant function is compression rather than elevation, and many patients with isolated supraspinatus tears abduct fully.

The teaching matters because it frames cuff dysfunction as the loss of one movement, which it is not.

q: What does cuff dysfunction actually produce clinically?
a:
Loss of a fulcrum — painful, inefficient, substituted movement with a shrugging pattern — rather than frank paralysis.

Without cuff compression holding the head centred, deltoid translates the head superiorly instead of rotating it about a fixed centre. The patient can often still get the arm up; what they cannot do is get it up efficiently or without pain.

q: Describe the coronal force couple and the consequence of its failure.
a:
Deltoid's superior pull balanced by the inferior cuff — lower fibres of subscapularis, infraspinatus and teres minor.

Failure gives unopposed deltoid, producing superior migration, loss of the fulcrum, and pseudoparalysis in the extreme. This is the couple whose failure shows up as a reduced acromiohumeral interval on radiograph.

q: Describe the transverse force couple and why it is critical for tear function.
a:
Subscapularis anteriorly balanced by infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly. Imbalance produces anteroposterior instability of the head during rotation.

This is the couple that must stay balanced for a tear to remain functional. It explains why an anteroposteriorly balanced tear can be surprisingly well tolerated, while an unbalanced one — a tear extending into subscapularis or infraspinatus — is not.

q: What are the scapula's four mechanical contributions?
a:
Upward rotation keeps the glenoid under the humeral head as the arm elevates. Posterior tilt elevates the acromion away from the cuff. External rotation maintains the glenohumeral relationship. And it provides a stable base for the cuff's origin.

Failure of each produces a specific problem: loss of the stable base at the top of range; reduced subacromial clearance; altered joint contact; and a cuff working from a moving platform.

q: What is the single fact that justifies scapular training, and what limits that argument?
a:
The cuff originates on the scapula — and a muscle cannot produce stable compression if its origin is unstable. That is the mechanical rationale for serratus anterior and lower trapezius work, rather than a general enthusiasm for "posture".

The limit: scapular dyskinesis is common in asymptomatic people and its association with pain is weaker than commonly taught. Train the scapula because the symptom-modification test was positive, not because it looked unusual.

q: State the scapulohumeral rhythm and its caveat.
a:
Elevation to 180° is roughly 120° glenohumeral and 60° scapular upward rotation — the conventional 2:1 ratio. For every 3° of arm elevation, about 2° is glenohumeral and 1° scapulothoracic.

The caveat: 2:1 is a teaching approximation, not a constant. Contributions vary with phase, plane, load, speed and individual, and the first 30° is predominantly glenohumeral, with the scapular share increasing through the arc.

q: What is the scapular plane, and why do we test and load in it?
a:
At rest the scapula sits on the posterolateral thorax, oriented about 30–45° anterior to the coronal plane. That orientation defines the scapular plane — "scaption".

We work in it because there the capsule is relatively untwisted, the cuff muscles have favourable lines of pull, and there is less soft-tissue compression than in pure coronal abduction. It is the plane the shoulder is built to work in, and therefore the default for both testing and loading.

q: Explain the shoulder's mechanical disadvantage with numbers.
a:
The arm is a 60–70 cm lever while the muscles acting on it have moment arms of only 2–3 cm — roughly a 20:1 disadvantage. Holding 1 kg in the hand therefore requires something like 20–30 kg of muscle force.

The arm alone is 4–5% of body weight (3–4 kg), and held horizontally the joint reaction force approaches body weight; instrumented prostheses record peaks from 50% to over 170% of body weight during elevation.

q: Name the four factors that multiply cuff demand.
a:
1) Elevation angle — demand rises steeply from the side toward 90°. 2) Lever length — straightening the elbow roughly doubles torque for the same weight. 3) External load — multiplied by the 20:1 disadvantage. 4) Time — sustained positions accumulate load and fatigue the cuff, degrading compression exactly when it is most needed.

Patients change all four without noticing, which is why a long shift is often more provocative than a heavy lift.

q: How can you progress or regress an exercise without changing the weight?
a:
By changing position and lever: supine → supported upright → scaption below 90° → full range → overhead → overhead with time under load.

Two consequences follow. Unloaded range-of-motion work is not a null stimulus — a 4 kg arm at 90° is a real demand for a deconditioned tendon, which is why supine is often the right starting point. And the elbow is your fastest dial: bending it halves the torque, regressing an exercise without the patient feeling they have gone backwards.

q: Name the three stages of the continuum model and what characterises each.
a:
Reactive — the tissue is over-responding, cells in an exaggerated state of activity, swelling without matrix breakdown. Dysrepair — the tendon has attempted repair and it is going wrong: more cells, more proteoglycan, collagen separating and losing alignment, early new vessels with nerve fibres alongside. Degenerative — established breakdown, with areas of cell death, disorganised matrix and extensive neovascularity.

These are not simply severity grades — they call for different doses, which is the entire point of the model.

q: How should a reactive tendon be loaded, and why?
a:
Reduce the load. The tissue is already over-responding, with cells in an exaggerated state of activity — load it heavily and you drive that response further, producing more proteoglycan, more swelling and more pain.

Use isometrics as a tolerable way of keeping it loaded without moving through provocative range, allow one to three weeks, then build. This is the one stage where backing off is the correct first move.

q: How should a tendon in dysrepair be loaded?
a:
Start graded loading now and progress it. This is the stage with the most to gain: the tissue is actively remodelling and the process is salvageable.

Typically this is weeks to months of symptoms, with the aggravating activity having usually continued throughout — so identifying and modifying that ongoing load is as important as the exercise you add.

q: How should a degenerative tendon be loaded, and what is the main error?
a:
Load it properly. You cannot fix the hole, but you do not need to — the abnormal area is surrounded by normal tendon that adapts perfectly well.

The main error at this stage is underdosing, usually because a scan report frightened someone. This is the patient most likely to be treated too gently on the strength of imaging that describes age-expected change.

q: Explain the doughnut and the hole.
a:
In a degenerative tendon the degenerate area is the hole — it will not be restored, and nothing you prescribe will restore it. But most of the tendon's cross-section is doughnut: normal tissue surrounding the lesion, which adapts to load perfectly well.

So you are not repairing the hole, you are strengthening the ring. This is the single most useful image for explaining to a frightened patient — and a frightened clinician — why a degenerative tendon on imaging should still be loaded properly.

q: How do you actually stage a patient on the continuum in clinic?
a:
You do not, precisely. You cannot biopsy them, and imaging cannot reliably stage them either.

What you do instead is assess irritability — how little it takes to provoke, how long it takes to settle, whether there is rest and night pain. That maps onto the continuum closely enough to be useful, and it has the advantage of being free, repeatable, and current at every visit rather than frozen at the date of a scan.

q: What is "reactive-on-degenerative", and why is it the commonest PM&R presentation?
a:
An older tendon with established degenerative change that has been acutely overloaded. Clinically: a long background of niggling discomfort punctuated by a recent sharp deterioration after an identifiable event.

It is common in a PM&R clinic because that is exactly the population — older tendons, long histories, and a recent spike that finally brought them in.

q: What is the trap in reactive-on-degenerative presentations?
a:
The imaging and history say degenerative — load it heavily, while the shoulder in front of you is acutely reactive.

Treat the reactive component first — relative rest and isometrics for one to three weeks — and only then build capacity in the degenerative substrate. Going straight to heavy loading here is the single commonest reason a well-intentioned programme flares and the patient disengages.

q: Why is "tendinitis" the wrong word? Give the histological findings.
a:
Because tendinopathic tissue shows degenerative, not inflammatory, change: collagen disorganisation with fibre thinning and loss of crimp; increased ground substance and proteoglycan content with water uptake (hence the swelling); and neovascularisation with accompanying neural ingrowth.

The term also misdirects treatment toward anti-inflammatories rather than load, which is the practical cost of using it.

q: Why does pain often begin in the dysrepair stage?
a:
Because the tissue is acquiring a nerve supply it does not normally have. New vessels grow in with nerve fibres alongside them.

Normal tendon is relatively poorly innervated; a tendon in dysrepair is not. This is the structural explanation for why symptoms can appear well after the loading change that caused the problem.

q: Which structure is probably the single biggest contributor to pain, and why does that matter?
a:
The subacromial–subdeltoid bursa — synovial tissue, densely innervated, sitting directly on top of the tendon and under the arch. In cuff disease it thickens, becomes irritated, and is compressed every time the arm elevates.

It matters because it explains why a subacromial corticosteroid injection can produce rapid relief in a condition whose underlying problem is tendon capacity: you have treated the bursa, not the tendon, and the capacity problem is unchanged when the injection wears off.

q: State the conceptual point about pain that underlies the whole chapter.
a:
Pain is an output, not a tissue readout. It is produced by the nervous system weighing nociceptive input together with context — expectation, threat value, sleep, mood, and what the patient has been told about their scan.

This is why two people with identical imaging can have completely different experiences, and why the consultation itself changes outcomes. The explanation you give is part of the treatment, not a preamble to it.

q: Describe the load–pain relationship in a typical tendon problem.
a:
A given activity produces a reasonably reproducible amount of pain, often with a characteristic 24-hour latency — worse the next morning rather than during the activity itself.

This is your most useful diagnostic signal, and it is free. Its reproducibility is what allows the pain rule to work as a self-regulation tool between appointments.

q: What does it mean when the load–pain relationship breaks down?
a:
When pain is unpredictable, unrelated to load, widespread, or accompanied by marked distress and sleep disturbance, you are no longer managing a pure capacity problem.

The programme must still be loaded, but it needs pacing, education about sensitisation, sleep management and often psychological input — and you should expect progress measured in a different currency, with function rather than pain score as the outcome.

q: Why do tears propagate rather than heal?
a:
Before the tear, load was spread across the full width of tendon. Once fibres are lost, their share is redistributed to the fibres at the edge of the defect — so the same external load produces higher local strain at the tear margin.

The edge is the weakest point and is being asked to carry more than before. It is also why larger defects enlarge more readily: a bigger hole concentrates more strain at its edge.

q: Describe the characteristic pain pattern.
a:
Lateral deltoid pain, often poorly localised, sometimes radiating to the deltoid insertion but rarely below the elbow. A painful arc classically 60–120°. Night pain, especially lying on the affected side — frequently the most disabling single feature and often the presenting complaint.

Onset is usually gradual, with an identifiable change in load behind it.

q: What should the character of weakness and stiffness be in cuff tendinopathy?
a:
Weakness, if present, is usually pain-inhibited rather than structural. Stiffness is mild and end-range.

Both have diagnostic value when they depart from this: weakness disproportionate to pain suggests structural failure or a neurological cause, and global stiffness points elsewhere — particularly to adhesive capsulitis.

q: Which functional losses do patients report, and what do they map onto?
a:
Patients do not say "I've lost external rotation." They say they cannot reach a back pocket, fasten a bra or tuck in a shirt (internal rotation and extension); reach a seatbelt or turn the wheel (external rotation); wash or dry their hair (abduction with external rotation); or reach a high shelf or hang washing (elevation).

Translating these back into movements is faster than a range chart — and it gives you the functional discharge targets at the same time.

q: Define irritability.
a:
Irritability has three components: how little it takes to provoke, how severe it gets, and how long it takes to settle.

It is a state, not a trait — it changes week to week, so it must be reassessed at each visit rather than assumed from the last one.

q: Why is irritability the single most practically useful assessment?
a:
Because irritability sets the dose while diagnosis sets the direction.

Every patient in this chapter has the same diagnosis; what differs is how much load the shoulder will currently accept. That is the variable that determines what you actually write on the programme, and it is free to measure.

q: Describe high irritability and its starting approach.
a:
Pain at rest; night pain every night; provoked by minimal activity such as dressing or light reaching; takes hours to settle; active range limited by pain well before passive end-range.

→ Settle first. Isometrics, pain-free range, sleep positioning and activity modification; consider a short NSAID course or an injection as a window. Avoid provocative loading for 1–3 weeks.

q: Describe moderate irritability and its starting approach.
a:
Pain with moderate activity; some night pain; settles within an hour; active range near passive.

→ Load cautiously but genuinely. Light-to-moderate isotonic loading through tolerable range, 2–3 sets, progressing every 1–2 weeks. The word "genuinely" matters — this patient is often under-loaded out of caution.

q: Describe low irritability, its starting approach, and the main risk.
a:
Pain only with heavy or sustained load; no night pain; settles quickly; full range.

→ Load properly. Heavy slow resistance, higher loads, add range, add speed. The main risk here is no longer flare-up — it is underdosing. These are the patients given a band and three sets of fifteen, who improve marginally and are then recorded as having failed conservative management when they were never adequately treated.

q: What is the relationship between active and passive range in cuff disease, and why is it the key discriminator?
a:
In rotator cuff disease passive range is preserved — the patient may not lift the arm, but you can lift it for them, because the restriction is pain and weakness rather than a mechanical block.

In adhesive capsulitis you cannot lift it either. This single comparison separates the two conditions more reliably than any special test, and it should be made before anything else in the examination.

q: What should be used to measure range of motion, and what should not?
a:
An inclinometer, goniometer or smartphone goniometer application — graded A in the 2025 guideline.

Not visual estimation. And note the explicit exception: scapular range measures are unreliable and have limited validity, and should not be used to measure dynamic scapular ROM.

q: What should be used to measure strength, and why not manual muscle testing?
a:
A hand-held dynamometer, in a standardised position — also grade A.

Manual muscle testing cannot detect the side-to-side deficits and incremental gains that tell you whether capacity is rising. Those numbers are the outcome measure of the entire programme; without them you have an impression, and impressions discharge patients too early.

q: What does a lag sign mean mechanically?
a:
You passively place the arm in a position — removing the demand to move — and the patient cannot hold it. That indicates loss of force transmission, a structural tear, because pain inhibition rarely prevents holding a position already achieved.

This is why lag signs outperform the pain-provocation tests: they indicate structural failure rather than sensitisation.

q: What are the test properties of lag signs, and how should that change your interpretation?
a:
Specific but not sensitive.

A positive is highly informative and should change the pathway toward imaging and a surgical opinion. A negative does not exclude a tear, particularly a small one — it means only that you have no positive reason to chase one today.

q: What is the real diagnostic value of the provocation tests?
a:
Modest. Combinations improve accuracy only marginally over single tests, and the accuracy studies used surgical findings in secondary-care populations as the reference standard — not tendinopathy as it is defined clinically.

The best of them: painful arc to confirm, Hawkins-Kennedy to rule out (grade B) — but both likelihood ratios are small. Do not rely on clinical test results alone to diagnose.

q: Why can rotator cuff special tests not be interpreted in a stiff shoulder?
a:
Because they are all positive when the capsule is tight. Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer, the empty and full can all provoke pain at end range in any shoulder that cannot reach end range comfortably.

This is a common source of a wrongly added second diagnosis — a patient with adhesive capsulitis labelled as having concurrent impingement because every test hurt. Establish passive range first; if it is restricted, the special tests tell you nothing.

q: Why is the full can preferred over the empty can?
a:
The full can (thumb up) produces supraspinatus activation comparable to the empty can while narrowing the subacromial space less and provoking less pain. As a loaded exercise there is no reason to choose the more provocative option for no additional benefit.

The distinction to keep: the empty can retains a role as a test (Jobe's). It is as an exercise that it is indefensible.

q: What should you watch during scapular assessment, and which tests are worth doing?
a:
Watch the lowering phase, not just the lift — eccentric control fails first.

Useful additions: the scapular assistance and scapular retraction tests; a wall press or push-up plus for serratus integrity; pectoralis minor length measured supine as how far the acromion rests off the plinth; and available thoracic extension in sitting.

q: What earns scapular work a place in the programme?
a:
A test that changes this patient's symptoms now — not an unusual appearance.

Dyskinesis is found in roughly 55–61% of overhead athletes and 33% of non-overhead athletes, and in general populations the rates in symptomatic and asymptomatic people are not meaningfully different. Appearance is therefore a poor guide; a positive scapular assistance or retraction test is a demonstrated contribution.

q: What four questions should the examination answer?
a:
Is it the cuff at all? (cervical screen, active versus passive range, pattern of weakness) → the diagnosis. Is there structural failure? (lag signs, trauma history, weakness disproportionate to pain) → the referral decision. How irritable is it? → the starting dose. What is the target load? (job, sport, life) → the endpoint.

If you can state all four at the end of the examination, you can write the prescription.

q: What is the single most useful product of the examination?
a:
The specific position and load that was comfortable in clinic — which becomes exercise one, written in those exact words.

It is individualised by a demonstrated test rather than a template, and the patient leaves having already succeeded at it once in front of you, which does more for adherence than any amount of explanation.

q: What does painless weakness suggest?
a:
A neurological cause — suprascapular neuropathy, C5 radiculopathy, neuralgic amyotrophy or motor neuron disease.

Tendinopathy weakness hurts. Weakness disproportionate to pain, or accompanied by wasting out of keeping with disuse, belongs to a different workup entirely rather than to a more aggressive cuff programme.

q: What does severe pain preceding patchy weakness suggest?
a:
Neuralgic amyotrophy — days of intense pain, then profound and often patchy weakness emerging as the pain settles.

The sequence is the clue: in cuff disease weakness and pain travel together, whereas here the pain leads and then hands over to weakness.

q: Why must the cervical spine be screened in every shoulder presentation?
a:
Because C5 radiculopathy often has no neck pain at all.

Waiting for the patient to volunteer neck symptoms before examining the neck is precisely how radiculopathy gets managed as cuff disease for months. The screen is quick — active cervical movement, Spurling's, a dermatomal and myotomal check — and the cost of omitting it is measured in wasted months.

q: Besides adhesive capsulitis, what else belongs on the differential list?
a:
Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (older, crepitus, radiographic change); locked posterior dislocation (seizure, electrocution or trauma — requires an axillary view, and classically missed); acute calcific tendinopathy (abrupt, severe, out-of-keeping pain with a deposit on radiograph); and polymyalgia rheumatica (over 50, bilateral girdle involvement, raised inflammatory markers).

A shoulder that is not improving at all is a diagnosis worth revisiting, not just a treatment to escalate.

q: When is "not yet" the right answer to imaging, and what is the threshold?
a:
Almost always at first presentation. The guideline recommends against ordering imaging to confirm rotator cuff tendinopathy in initial management, and suggests considering it if symptoms have not resolved or improved within a maximum of 12 weeks of appropriate non-surgical management.

"Appropriate" is doing real work in that sentence: scanning a patient who has done four weeks of light band work is imaging an untreated patient, not a treatment failure.

q: What did the largest population-based MRI study find, and why does it matter?
a:
In 602 adults aged 41–76 from a nationally representative sample, 98.7% had a rotator cuff abnormality — tendinopathy 25%, partial-thickness tear 62%, full-thickness tear 11%. Only 1.3% were normal, and just 18% reported current symptoms.

It establishes that an abnormal cuff is close to a normal finding in adults. The question is never is there an abnormality — it is does this abnormality explain this patient's pain, and imaging cannot answer that.

q: In that study, how did symptomatic and asymptomatic shoulders compare?
a:
Abnormalities were present in 96% of asymptomatic and 98% of symptomatic shoulders — a difference of 1.8% (95% CI −2.9 to 4.7). And 78% of all full-thickness tears (75 of 96) were in shoulders that did not hurt.

This is the single most useful comparison to have ready for the imaging conversation with a patient.

q: What happened to the association between full-thickness tear and symptoms after adjustment?
a:
It disappeared once other structural findings and positive clinical tests were accounted for.

The authors' reading: clinical examination is a better guide to current symptoms than imaging. That belongs in your examination teaching as much as in your imaging teaching.

q: Below what age were no full-thickness tears found, and what does that change?
a:
45. Prevalence rose from 4% at ages 45–49 to 28% at 70 and over.

So a full-thickness tear in a patient under 45 is not an age-related incidental finding — it is traumatic until proven otherwise, and that shifts the pathway toward early surgical referral rather than a three-month loading trial.

q: Which imaging modality should be prioritised, and why?
a:
Ultrasound first — lower cost with diagnostic properties similar to MRI for confirming a cuff disorder.

It is also dynamic, allows immediate bilateral comparison, and can guide an injection in the same sitting — none of which a static MRI offers. Its main limitation is operator dependence.

q: How do ultrasound, MRI and MR arthrography compare for detecting tears?
a:
For full-thickness tears they are essentially equivalent: MRI 94%/93%, MR arthrography 94%/92%, ultrasound 92%/93% — no significant difference (p = 0.7).

For partial-thickness tears, none performs well. Choose on cost, access and what else you need to see — which in practice means ultrasound first.

q: What is the magic angle artefact, and how do you test for it?
a:
Where supraspinatus curves over the humeral head, its fibres sit near 55° to the main magnetic field, and ordered collagen at that angle produces artificially increased signal on short-TE sequences — T1, proton density, gradient echo.

It is the commonest false-positive "tendinosis" on a shoulder MRI. The test: real pathology persists on long-TE T2; magic angle signal disappears. If a report describes tendinosis seen only on PD, ask whether it was confirmed on T2.

q: Which element of the imaging report carries the most prognostic weight, and what are its grades?
a:
The Goutallier grade of fatty infiltration: 0 normal muscle; 1 some fatty streaks; 2 fatty atrophy under 50%; 3 around 50%; 4 over 50%.

Grades 3–4 predict markedly poorer functional recovery after repair, and unlike tear size, fatty infiltration is largely irreversible — repairing the tendon does not restore the muscle. A 2 cm tear with Goutallier 4 is a worse shoulder than a 4 cm tear with Goutallier 1. Read the muscle before the tendon.

q: State the Cofield tear-size categories and the Ellman partial-thickness grades.
a:
Cofield (full-thickness, by size): small <1 cm; medium 1–3 cm; large 3–5 cm; massive >5 cm, also commonly defined as involving two or more tendons.

Ellman (partial-thickness, by depth): grade 1 <3 mm (~<25%); grade 2 3–6 mm (~25–50%); grade 3 >6 mm (>50%). Located as articular-sided, bursal-sided or intrasubstance — intrasubstance being the most common in cadaveric work and the hardest to detect.

q: What are the four targets of treatment?
a:
Settle the symptoms. Build capacity. Restore the task. Change what the patient believes about their shoulder.

The fourth is not an optional extra: a patient who believes their tendon is torn and fragile will not load it, whatever is written on the programme.

q: What is the governing principle of treatment?
a:
Load is the treatment; everything else buys a window.

No adjunct raises capacity, so the ceiling on any adjunct's value is how much loading it unlocks. Judge each one by a single question: does this let the patient load sooner, heavier or more consistently? If not, it is costing time.

q: Name the five education messages.
a:
Capacity not damage · loading is the treatment · pain is allowed within the rule · months not weeks · the scan finding is normal for your age.

The scan message blocks everything behind it. A patient who believes they have a tear will not accept that the problem is capacity, will not load the shoulder, and will not wait months when an operation appears available. Clear the imaging belief first — ideally before they read the report alone at home.

q: How should the condition be explained to a patient, and what should you avoid drawing?
a:
As a mismatch, not damage — the tendon has been asked for more than it can currently give. Name their own spike, so the onset stops feeling random. Then say the part that matters most: both sides of the mismatch can be changed.

Avoid drawing the acromion with the tendon running underneath. That picture teaches impingement, which is the belief you are trying to remove. If you draw anything, draw two lines — demand and capacity — and show them crossing.

q: State the pain rule given to patients.
a:
Up to about 5/10 during the exercise · settled by the next morning · not rising week to week.

All three parts matter: the threshold, the 24-hour response, and the weekly trend — the last of which catches a programme going wrong when the first two still look acceptable. Give them the rule, not just the exercise; it converts them from someone who stops at the first twinge into someone who can self-regulate between appointments.

q: Where does the pain rule come from, and what is the caveat?
a:
From Silbernagel's pain-monitoring model in Achilles tendinopathy, where patients who continued loading within these limits did no worse than those who rested for six weeks — and the resting group gained nothing from resting.

The caveat: no equivalent rotator cuff trial validates these thresholds. They are pragmatic clinical guides extrapolated from another tendon, not validated biological cut-offs.

q: What does the 2025 guideline grade A, and what does it deliberately omit?
a:
Prescribing an active rehabilitation exercise programme as initial treatment, which may include motor control and/or resistance training with various loads — notably without specifying the dose, because the trial evidence does not support specifying it.

That omission is the honest position, not an oversight. You are not choosing between protocols with different efficacy; you are applying the principles of tissue adaptation to an individual.

q: Which exercise type is superior for rotator cuff related shoulder pain?
a:
None. Systematic reviews consistently find no clear superiority among eccentric, concentric, isometric and heavy slow resistance.

Comparisons of higher versus lower dose show possible benefit for function with higher doses, at low certainty and with no clear effect on pain. The specific exercises matter far less than how they are dosed and progressed.

q: If no exercise type is superior, what is the active ingredient?
a:
Progression and resistance.

Progressive resisted exercise significantly reduces pain (MD −1.07/10 against basic advice, placebo detuned laser or no treatment). Non-progressive and non-resisted exercise do not beat a sham (MD −0.33/10, 95% CI −0.81 to 0.15). That contrast is the strongest argument for every dosing rule that follows.

q: What is "failed physiotherapy" usually, and what three questions expose it?
a:
A failed dose, not a failed treatment.

Ask: What load were they actually lifting? How often? And did it ever increase? Four sessions of pendulums and a yellow band over six weeks is not a trial of rehabilitation — it is a reason to start one. This matters because "failed conservative management" is the phrase that unlocks imaging, injection and surgical referral, and it is frequently untrue.

q: Name the four rehabilitation phases with their objectives and approximate timeframes.
a: 1) Initial loading — control symptoms, establish tolerable loading; isometrics, light resistance, comfortable range; weeks 0–2. 2) Progressive strengthening — improve cuff and scapular strength; isotonic resistance, controlled elevation; weeks 2–6. 3) Advanced strengthening — load tolerance, endurance, overhead capacity; heavier resistance, longer levers, overhead loading; weeks 6–12. 4) Return to activity — occupational or sporting demands; task-specific loading, endurance, power; week 12 onward.

q: What is the critical caveat to the phase timeframes?
a:
They are illustrative, not validated milestones. The stages are states, not weeks.

A patient enters a stage when they meet its entry criteria and leaves when they meet the next one's. Two patients with the same diagnosis can be in different stages on the same day; phases overlap; low-irritability patients may begin progressive strengthening immediately; and a patient can move backwards after a flare.

q: Who needs stage 1, and who does not?
a:
It is for a genuinely irritable shoulder — pain at rest or at night, provoked by light or brief activity, taking hours to settle, or recently flared including reactive-on-degenerative.

Most patients do not need it. Starting everyone here by reflex delays treatment by three weeks and teaches the patient their shoulder is fragile. Low-irritability patients may begin isotonic strengthening immediately, and isometrics are an option, not a mandatory first stage.

q: What is the goal of stage 1 — and what is it not?
a:
The goal is to establish a level of loading the patient can perform consistently without sustained symptom exacerbation, while reducing irritability and maintaining mobility.

It is not to eliminate pain before starting exercise. Waiting for pain-free is the commonest reason stage 1 becomes permanent, because that threshold may never arrive.

q: What is the evidence for isometrics as an analgesic?
a:
Weak. The original effect — a 4.3-point immediate pain drop — came from six athletes with patellar tendinopathy. Follow-ups found progressively smaller effects (1.8, then 0.9 points), and one group found −0.3 points in the opposite direction.

A meta-analysis of 10 trials and 294 participants concluded isometrics are not superior to isotonic exercise for tendinopathy pain, immediately or in the short term.

q: Given that evidence, what is the honest reason to use isometrics?
a:
Because they are a tolerable way to keep an irritable tendon loaded without moving through provocative range — not because they switch pain off.

The practical corollary: do not keep a patient in stage 1 waiting for analgesia that may not arrive. Exit on criteria, not on the disappearance of pain.

q: Give a typical stage 1 isometric dose.
a:
5 holds × 30–45 seconds at about 70% effort, 30–60 seconds rest, once or twice daily, using one or two positions chosen from what was comfortable in clinic.

Coach the effort by instruction rather than by number: "push as hard as you can — that's ten; now ease back to about seven. You should be working, but able to breathe and talk."

q: How do you progress within stage 1 before moving on?
a:
Three dials: duration (15–20 s → 30 s → 45 s), effort (40–50% → 70%), and most usefully angle — moving the hold from the most comfortable position toward the provocative one.

The angle progression is the one most often forgotten, and it is the most valuable: isometric strength gains are largely angle-specific, so moving the hold toward the range stage 2 will demand both prepares the shoulder and gives you a clean reason to progress.

q: What arrives in stage 2 that was absent in stage 1?
a:
Three things at once: movement through range, the eccentric (lowering) phase where tendon strain is highest, and exposure to the whole available arc including the provocative part.

The eccentric is the real step up — an isometric asks the cuff to hold; an isotonic asks it to control a load on the way down, which is what most daily tasks actually demand. Warn the patient to expect more symptom response in the first fortnight here than anywhere else, so they read it correctly rather than as deterioration.

q: Give the stage 2 dose.
a:
3–4 sets × 10–15 reps, about 3 s out and 3 s back, 60–90 s rest, three times weekly, at a load where the last 2–3 reps are genuinely hard.

Three sessions a week with real load beats five with compromised load — the frequency exists to leave recovery between sessions, not for any collagen-timing reason.

q: Why does slow tempo matter?
a:
Four reasons that compound. It removes momentum, so the muscle rather than the swing does the work. It makes the eccentric deliberate rather than a drop. It increases time under tension at a given load. And it is self-limiting — a weight that cannot be lowered over three seconds is too heavy.

That last point gives the patient a rule for choosing loads without you in the room.

q: How do you set the starting load?
a:
Find a weight they can complete 15 controlled repetitions with, where the last two or three are hard. If 15 is easy it is too light; if they cannot reach 10 with control it is too heavy.

The load must be meaningful. Tissue adapts to mechanical magnitude, and a resistance producing no sense of effort produces no adaptive signal — the commonest reason a conscientious programme achieves nothing.

q: What changes when 3 × 15 becomes comfortable?
a:
The load goes up — not the repetitions.

Drifting to three sets of twenty-five converts strength work into endurance work, and the programme quietly stops building anything. Change one variable at a time, in order of preference: load, then range, then position.

q: Name the core stage 2 exercises and the rationale for each.
a:
ER at 0° (towel under the elbow) — the posterior cuff is where the measurable deficit usually is, and it is the force-couple partner balancing deltoid's superior pull. Scaption / full can — the elevation task itself, in the plane the shoulder is built to work in. Row — posterior chain and scapular control under genuine load, carrying far more weight than band work. Press: landmine → incline → overhead — reaching the overhead task by angle rather than avoidance.

Add serratus anterior and lower trapezius work only if the scapular tests were positive.

q: Which progression within the programme is most often forgotten, and why does it matter?
a:
Moving external rotation from 0° out to 45°, then 90° of abduction.

ER strength at the side does not transfer to ER strength overhead, and overhead is where the demand lies. Abduction with external rotation is also the position patients most avoid, so re-entering it deliberately under load is strength work and graded exposure at once. A shoulder trained only at the side is not prepared for what its work or sport requires.

q: What is the commonest failure of a cuff programme, and what question exposes it?
a:
The load never changes. A patient doing three sets of fifteen with a yellow band in week two should not still be doing that in week eight — if they are, the programme is maintenance, not treatment.

At every review ask: what are you lifting now, and what were you lifting last time? If the answer is the same, fix that before considering anything else.

q: Why ask the patient to record their load?
a:
A simple note on a phone — date, exercise, weight, reps — does three things: it makes progression visible when pain is not yet improving; it tells you at review whether the dose actually increased; and it converts an abstract instruction into a measurable behaviour.

It is also the quickest way to discover that a "12-week trial of physiotherapy" involved the same green band throughout.

q: State the entry criteria for stage 3.
a:
3 × 15 comfortable at a load that means something; full available range trained including the formerly provocative arc; ER loaded in abduction, not only at the side; no next-morning flare, with symptoms stable or improving; and irritability low — the limiting factor is now strength, not pain.

That last line is the real criterion. If pain still dictates the dose, the patient is in stage 2.

q: Name the four goals of stage 3.
a: 1) Close the strength deficit against the uninvolved side — "feels better" is not a discharge criterion. 2) Build tolerance to heavy load near end range, because the demands that break shoulders combine high load with disadvantageous position. 3) Build endurance and repetitive load tolerance — a patient may lift a weight once but fail after repeated overhead movements. 4) Introduce faster and more complex movements, as task-specific additions rather than mandatory components.

q: Which exercises characterise stage 3, and what must be kept in?
a:
Overhead press (ribs down, no lumbar arch to fake range), ER at 90° abduction loaded, row with full scapular travel, pull-down → pull-up progression with eccentric emphasis, bench or incline press, loaded carries including overhead carry, and heavier scaption or lateral raise with controlled descent.

Keep the ER work in. It is the specific deficit, and no compound lift trains it — which is exactly why it tends to disappear from programmes at this stage.

q: Who needs stage 4, and who does not?
a:
Needed by those whose work or sport demands speed, elasticity or repeated overhead power — throwers, swimmers, racquet and volleyball players, climbers, gymnasts, and manual workers who apply force quickly (hammering, scaffolding, catching, lifting awkward loads).

Not needed by a 70-year-old whose goal is a kitchen shelf, or a desk worker who can press, row and carry at full load. For them, stage 3 is the finish line, and adding stage 4 wastes their time.

q: When should a programme be regressed?
a:
When symptoms do not settle within 24 hours; when morning pain or stiffness is worse week on week; or when the patient compensates — shrugging, trunk lean, breath-holding — to complete repetitions.

Note what is not on that list: discomfort during the exercise, which the pain rule explicitly permits.

q: How should a flare be handled, and why is stopping wrong?
a:
Reduce the load by 20–30% and rebuild, rather than stopping. A flare means the dose exceeded current capacity, so the correct response is a smaller dose, not no dose.

Stopping teaches the patient that loading is dangerous, costs the capacity already gained, and usually means restarting two weeks later from a lower baseline. Tell them this at the first appointment, so the inevitable bad week does not end the treatment.

q: Give the troubleshooting sequence for a programme not working at 6–8 weeks.
a:
Work through it in order before concluding rehabilitation has failed:

  1. Is the diagnosis right? (missed cervical, neurological, inflammatory, calcific, adhesive capsulitis, instability)
  2. Has the load actually increased? — the commonest finding.
  3. Is it being done? Simplify to three exercises; agree a minimum dose.
  4. What is happening outside the programme? The unmodified provocative load — the job, the baby, the gym class; exercises cannot out-compete it.
  5. Is the tendon reactive? Step back to stage 1 for 1–2 weeks.
  6. Is the background hostile? HbA1c, smoking, sleep, thyroid, weight, mood.
  7. Is sensitisation dominant?
  8. Only now, consider imaging and procedures.

q: How should every adjunct be judged?
a:
By whether it lets the patient load sooner, heavier or more consistently.

None of them raise capacity, so the ceiling on any adjunct's value is how much loading it unlocks. Load treats the cause; adjuncts treat the week. Name the window each one buys, give it an end date, and never let it displace the loading in the patient's mind.

q: What is the single finding that answers most adjunct questions?
a:
Ultrasound, low-level laser and PEMF added to exercise produce no clinically important additional benefit — Cochrane, 47 trials, 2,388 participants.

This is exactly what the mechanism predicts: these modalities do not deliver mechanical load of the magnitude tissue adapts to, so whatever they do, they cannot be treating the problem.

q: What is the guideline position on therapeutic ultrasound?
a:
Should not be used — grade C in calcific disease, grade B in non-calcific, alone or added to an active rehabilitation programme.

The stronger evidence is against its use in ordinary non-calcific tendinopathy, which is the presentation you see most. This is one of the clearest negative recommendations in the guideline.

q: Where do shockwave and laser have a role, and what is the caveat?
a:
Calcific disease only. Shockwave may be used for calcific tendinopathy (C) and is recommended against for non-calcific (C); laser is supported for calcific only (C). The one-line summary: shockwave and laser are for the calcium, not the tendon.

The caveat worth carrying: Cochrane's 32-trial, 2,281-participant review found shockwave effects below clinical importance and no calcific-versus-non-calcific subgroup difference, so the split is less secure than the grades imply.

q: What is the grade and proper use of manual therapy?
a:
Grade B — spinal and/or upper limb manual therapy, alone or combined with exercise, for short-term pain reduction. It is the best-supported adjunct in the list.

Use it in the same session as the loading, as the thing that makes the next exercise tolerable: mobilise, then load, and let the patient feel the difference. Delivered as its own appointment it inverts the treatment — and the patient will draw the same conclusion about what is really treating them.

q: What are the grades for taping and acupuncture, and where does taping genuinely earn its place?
a:
Taping grade D — short-term pain reduction, conflicting evidence. Acupuncture grade C, added to an active rehabilitation programme.

Taping earns its place as a symptom-modification tool: if it changes what the patient can do today, you have both a tolerable exercise and a demonstration to them that their symptoms are modifiable. Use it for that, with an end date, not as a standing intervention.

q: What is the role, timing and limitation of corticosteroid injection?
a:
May be used (grade B) for pain and short-term disability, but not first-line (grade C), and with ultrasound guidance where available (grade B).

The limitation is the time course: benefit is short term only, up to about 8 weeks, with no difference at medium or long term — and exercise beats injection in the medium term. Its legitimate role is to buy a window in which loading becomes possible, with the programme starting during that window rather than after it. Rare but real adverse effects: tendon rupture and infection.

q: What is the best-supported procedure for calcific disease?
a:
Ultrasound-guided lavage (barbotage) — grade B, for calcific tendinopathy refractory to initial treatment. It outperformed shockwave for both pain and calcification size in the long term.

The sequence: confirm the deposit on radiograph → standard loading programme and education → subacromial corticosteroid if pain prevents loading → lavage if refractory → shockwave as the alternative where lavage is unavailable. Its efficacy as a first treatment, or in acute cases, has not been demonstrated.

q: What did the placebo-controlled trials and Cochrane find about subacromial decompression?
a:
CSAW: decompression was no better than placebo arthroscopy at 6 months (Oxford Shoulder Score −1.3, 95% CI −3.9 to 1.3). FIMPACT reached the same conclusion at 5 years, and found no benefit over exercise either. Cochrane rates this high-certainty evidence of no clinically important benefit.

Note the pattern across this literature: the negative findings are the high-certainty ones; the positive findings sit at low to very low certainty.

q: What does the evidence show for surgical repair of rotator cuff tears, and what are its limits?
a:
Cochrane found probably little or no meaningful benefit of repair over exercise with or without injection at 12 months — pain 0.87/10 better, Constant score 5.98/100 better.

Two limits matter enormously. No placebo-surgery trial has ever been done for cuff repair. And most participants had small degenerative supraspinatus tears, so the finding does not transfer to traumatic tears, large tears or younger patients. Repair for the right tear still has a role.

q: Which patient-reported measures are recommended, and at what grade?
a:
SPADI, DASH/QuickDASH and ASES are named as suitable options. Using valid, reliable and responsive questionnaires to assess pain and disability is grade A in the 2025 guideline.

Choose one and use it consistently — switching instruments between visits destroys the comparison you were collecting it for.

q: Give the approximate MCIDs for the common shoulder measures, and how should they be used?
a:
SPADI ≈8–13 points · QuickDASH ≈8–15 · ASES ≈12–17 in cuff disease · Oxford Shoulder Score ≈4–6 · WORC ≈11–13% · Constant–Murley ≈10 points.

Treat these as approximate thresholds for "the patient would notice this", not precise cut-offs — values vary between studies and populations.

q: Give the physical benchmarks for return to heavy or overhead demand.
a:
Range symmetrical with the other side, by inclinometer rather than visual estimate. Isometric ER, IR and scaption strength on handheld dynamometry in a standardised position, with a limb symmetry index above 90%. ER:IR ratio roughly 0.65–0.75. Endurance matched to occupational demand. And the actual provocative task completed without next-day flare.

That last one is not a proxy — it is the full shift or the complete training session, not a gym exercise that resembles it.

q: When should measures be recorded, and what question do three data points answer?
a:
Baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks, the same way each time.

Three points answer the only question that matters at review: is capacity rising? If pain has not changed but ER strength has risen 30%, the programme is working and needs time. If neither has changed in eight weeks, work the troubleshooting sequence. "Better" is not an outcome — it will not survive a clinic letter, a return-to-work discussion or an insurance query.

q: On what timeline does tendon adapt, when do patients feel better, and why does the gap matter?
a:
Tendon adapts on roughly a 12-week timeline; patients feel better at about six weeks.

That gap is where relapse happens. The patient feels recovered while their capacity is still well short of their demands, stops, returns to full activity and flares — then concludes the treatment failed. Say it in advance, at the first appointment: said then it builds credibility and persistence; said afterwards it sounds like an excuse.

q: How do you answer "shouldn't I get a scan?"
a:
"We can, and sometimes we should. But at your age the scan will almost certainly show some wear, which is also true of people with no pain at all. It would change what you believe more than what we do. If you're not improving in about twelve weeks, that's the point at which the scan starts to earn its place."

The structure matters: it is not a refusal, it is a reframe with a timeline attached, which converts a dismissal into a plan the patient can hold you to.

q: Which factors predict persistent pain?
a:
Age over 55 (OR ~3.8) and perceived high job demand (OR ~4.1), together with delayed care after injury, prolonged symptom duration, greater restriction at presentation, and a compensation or litigation context.

Note that the strongest of these concern timing and work, not tissue — nothing on an MRI appears on this list.

q: Which commonly assumed prognostic factors do not predict persistence?
a:
Dominant versus non-dominant side, education level, comorbidities, pressure pain thresholds, perceived job control, and jobs requiring higher shoulder forces.

Also worth knowing: psychological factors predict outcome in surgically managed patients but not reliably in conservatively managed ones. Address distress because it affects adherence, not because the evidence shows it determines outcome.

q: What must accompany discharge, and why?
a:
A maintenance prescription: 1–2 strength sessions weekly, indefinitely, for anyone with ongoing overhead demands — two or three exercises including external rotation, since nothing in ordinary work or training loads it.

Capacity decays. A patient discharged with no ongoing loading drifts back toward the state in which they broke down, usually within months, and will describe the relapse as the treatment having failed. Frame it explicitly: this is not rehabilitation continuing, it is what preserves the margin you spent six months building.

q: Which presentation warrants early surgical referral rather than a trial of rehabilitation?
a:
Acute traumatic tear with marked weakness or a positive lag sign, particularly in a younger patient.

Refer early rather than rehabilitating for three months first: repair for the right tear still has a role, and delay costs reparability. This is the exception to the general rule that cuff problems get a loading programme.

q: What else should prompt referral or escalation?
a:
Severe persistent pain or disability despite a maximum of 12 weeks of appropriate non-surgical care; red flags for infection, malignancy or fracture; and significant neurological deficit.

The word "appropriate" carries the weight — escalating a patient who never had a properly dosed programme refers the wrong problem.

q: What follows a diagnosis of massive irreparable tear?
a:
Not the end of rehabilitation. The anterior deltoid programme restores useful function in many patients, by training the deltoid to substitute for lost cuff function and re-establish elevation without an intact cuff providing the fulcrum.

This matters because "irreparable" is routinely heard by patients — and sometimes by clinicians — as "untreatable", and the result is a patient discharged with nothing when a structured programme would have restored meaningful overhead function.
